summary: Describes a packet explosion problem that can happen with mutual encapsulation of protocols, where protocol A encapsulates B and B also encapsulates A. It is an informational warning about this design mistake.

plainLanguage.summary: Mutual encapsulation occurs when one protocol can carry another, and the second can also carry the first. RFC 1326 explains how a routing loop can repeatedly add headers, fragment packets, and cause a rapid increase in traffic.

subtitle: A warning that routing loops can make mutually encapsulated packets grow and multiply.

tldr.problem: When protocol A can encapsulate B and B can encapsulate A, a routing loop can cause packets to acquire repeated headers and grow.
tldr.mechanism: If encapsulation does not preserve hop counts, looping packets may not expire. They can reach the MTU, fragment, and continue looping, leading to an exponential increase in packets.
tldr.outcome: The informational memo warns against mutual encapsulation and discusses hop-count preservation and header inspection as possible mitigations, each with limitations.

today: RFC 1326 is an Informational memo, and the unit metadata lists no RFC as obsoleting or updating it. Its security section says security issues are not discussed.

sections.title: When Protocols Encapsulate Each Other
sections.content:
Encapsulation carries one protocol's packet inside another protocol's packet. It can help different networks interwork. RFC 1326 focuses on mutual encapsulation: protocol A carries B in some cases, while B carries A in others. The RFC gives IP over AppleTalk and AppleTalk over IP as examples.

The memo describes a danger that may arise when a routing loop combines with this arrangement. It provides information to the Internet community and does not specify an Internet standard.
sections.plainLanguage: Encapsulation puts one protocol's packet inside another protocol's packet. The risk described here appears when each protocol can carry the other and routing sends packets around a loop.

sections.title: How Packets Grow in a Routing Loop
sections.content:
In the RFC's example, routers connect backbones that use different protocols. A router wraps a packet in the protocol required by the next backbone; another router removes that outer header and forwards the packet. If routes form a loop, routers may instead repeatedly wrap the packet in alternating headers.

If each new encapsulation fails to preserve the previous header's hop count, the packet may never expire. It can grow until it reaches the Maximum Transmission Unit (MTU), the size limit for transmission on a link, and then fragment. The fragments can continue around the loop and fragment again. The RFC says this can cause an exponential explosion in looping packets and saturate links; the loop may then need manual intervention if routing and management packets are lost.
sections.plainLanguage: Each router in the loop can add another protocol header to a packet. Without preserved hop counts, packets may keep circulating, become too large, fragment, and create many more packets.

sections.title: Possible Ways to Reduce the Risk
sections.content:
One possible fix is to preserve hop-count information when adding a new header. This can stop packets from looping forever, but some protocols have no hop count, and different protocols use different ranges. The RFC notes that translating to a smaller range can discard packets on paths that are still valid.

Another idea is for routers to inspect headers for repeated encapsulation and discard packets that appear to be looping. This can fail when a router does not recognize an inner protocol, when packets are encrypted, or when multiple instances of the same header are legitimate. The memo suggests a hybrid response: prohibit nested mutual encapsulation where possible, use hop-count preservation and header inspection where appropriate, and generally discourage mutual encapsulation.
sections.plainLanguage: Keeping hop counts can limit loops, and inspecting headers can reveal repeated wrapping. Both methods have limits, so the memo recommends avoiding mutual encapsulation where possible.

references.text: Shoch, J., Cohen, D., and D. Taft, "Mutual Encapsulation of Internetwork Protocols", Computer Networks 5, North-Holland, 1981, pp. 287-300.
